brief: Orders arrive as ADD p (direction unknown) and ACCEPT p (remove the best BUY or SELL at p). Count the BUY/SELL assignments of the ADDs for which every step is valid, mod 1e9+7.
key_idea: At all times the sorted book is BUYs then SELLs, so the valid states form a gap position; the DP over gap positions only needs values stored on present prices, merged on ACCEPT.
solution:
1. Keep the present prices in an ordered set S and a value per gap, keyed by the gap's left boundary price (0 = start).
2. ADD p: its left gap stays, the new gap after p copies the value of the gap before p; total grows by that value.
3. ACCEPT p: the two gaps around p merge into one gap with their sum; every other gap dies (use a generation counter so stale values read as 0).
4. Total after the last action is the answer; if no assignment survives it is 0.
5. Edge cases: ACCEPT of the only present order; empty book.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run:
Sample 2: ADD1 -> gaps {start:1, 1:1}, total 2; ADD2 -> total 3; ADD3 -> total 4.
ACCEPT 2: merge gap(1)+gap(2) = 1+1 = 2, all others dead.
Answer 2 (matches sample).
note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. Verified against an exhaustive brute force on 300 random small logs.

brief: Given an n x m grid over {A,G,C,T}, change the fewest cells so every 2x2 block has all four letters. Output the nice grid.
key_idea: A nice grid is either row-periodic (rows alternate between two complementary letter pairs, each row alternating its two letters) or the transpose of that; each row's start letter can be chosen independently.
solution:
1. For each of the 3 ways to split {A,G,C,T} into two pairs and each order of the pairs on even/odd rows, build candidate rows.
2. For each row, try both start letters of its pair pattern and keep the one with fewer mismatches against the input row.
3. Sum the costs; keep the best pattern.
4. Run the same on the transposed grid and keep the cheaper of the two orientations.
5. Output the chosen grid.
dry_run:
Own example: 2x2 'AA','AA', pairs {A,G} on row 0 and {C,T} on row 1.
Row 0 start A gives 'AG' (cost 1); row 1 'CT' (cost 2).
Total cost 3; other pair choices are compared the same way.
note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. Brute force over all grids on random 2x2 to 3x3 cases agreed on the minimum cost.

brief: Connected weighted graph; you may add 1 to edge weights. Make the MST unique while keeping its total weight, using the fewest increments.
key_idea: Process equal-weight edge groups in order; edges that join different components form a multigraph on components, and every surplus edge beyond a spanning forest must be bumped by 1 (cost = candidates - successful unions).
solution:
1. Sort edges by weight; DSU over vertices.
2. For each group of equal weight: count edges whose endpoints are in different components at the start of the group (c).
3. Union all group edges, counting successful unions (k).
4. Add c - k to the answer.
5. Bumping by 1 never creates a tie that matters, since the next group weight is at least w+1 (standard editorial argument).
complexity: O(m log m) time, O(n + m) space

w=3: both edges cross components, c=2; one union succeeds, k=1, add 1.
Answer 1 (matches sample).

brief: Given next-greater indices for a hidden permutation (some entries -1 meaning unknown), output any permutation consistent with the known entries, or -1.
key_idea: Valid next pointers form a stack chain of prefix maxima; an unknown entry can safely be set to i+1 (the stack top), and each value is inserted just below its next-greater element in a value-ordered list.
solution:
1. Scan i from n down to 1 with a stack of indices (bottom is the sentinel n+1).
2. Let j = next_i, or i+1 if unknown. If j is not on the stack, answer -1.
3. Pop until j is on top, push i.
4. Insert i into the value order immediately below j (for j = n+1, at the top).
5. Read the value order from the bottom to assign 1..n.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space per test

brief: Projects each need rating >= a_i and change rating by b_i; the rating must stay non-negative. Decide whether all n projects can be completed in some order.
key_idea: Do all non-negative-b projects first in increasing a; then the negative ones in decreasing a+b.
solution:
1. Split projects into b >= 0 and b < 0.
2. Sort b >= 0 by a ascending; greedily take each if rating >= a.
3. Sort b < 0 by a+b descending; take each if rating >= a and rating + b >= 0.
4. Print YES if all were taken, else NO.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

brief: Given a binary string s, find a binary string t of equal length with the same longest-non-decreasing-subsequence value on every substring and the maximum number of zeros.
key_idea: Read 1 as an opening bracket and 0 as a closing bracket; a 1 that gets matched by a later 0 stays, and every unmatched 1 can become 0.
solution:
1. Scan left to right; push the index of each '1'.
2. On each '0', if the stack is non-empty, pop and mark that 1 as matched.
3. At the end every '1' not marked matched becomes '0'; other characters are unchanged.
4. Output t.

note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. Exhaustive brute force over all t for random strings of length <=8 agreed on validity and zero count; samples match exactly.

brief: Given two permutations p and q of positions, build a lowercase string of length n that is non-decreasing when read in p-order and in q-order and uses at least k distinct letters, or report NO.
key_idea: A prefix of p that is also a prefix of q is a cut; cuts split positions into blocks that can each take one letter, and the number of blocks is the maximum number of distinct letters.
solution:
1. Let qr[x] be the position of x in q.
2. Walk p; keep the running max of qr over the prefix. When that max equals the prefix length, it is a cut and the block index increments.
3. If the number of blocks is below k, print NO.
4. Else give each position the letter 'a' + min(block, k-1), which is non-decreasing in both orders.
dry_run: Sample: p=1 2 3, q=1 3 2, k=2. Prefix {1} is a cut (block 0). Prefix {1,2} is not (max qr = 3). Prefix {1,2,3} is a cut. Blocks {1},{2,3} give 'abb'.
note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. Brute force over all strings on alphabet size n for n<=5 agreed on existence and validity.

brief: N x N bulb grid with a fixed bar pattern b. Row r flips cells (r,j) by b_j; column c flips cells (i,c) by b_i. Find a sequence of applications turning the start grid into the target, or -1.
key_idea: Operations commute (XOR), so each row and column is used 0 or 1 times and the condition is D[i][j] = x_i*b_j xor y_j*b_i; fixing one pivot k with b_k=1 and guessing x_k,y_k determines every other variable.
solution:
1. D = start xor target. If b is all zero, answer 0 when D is zero, else -1.
2. Pick k with b_k = 1. For each of the 4 guesses of (x_k, y_k):
3. Set x_i = D[i][k] xor (y_k and b_i) and y_j = D[k][j] xor (x_k and b_j).
4. Verify x_i*b_j xor y_j*b_i == D[i][j] for all cells; if it holds, output the rows and columns with 1.
5. If no guess works, print -1.
dry_run: Sample 2: N=2, b=10, D=[[1,0],[0,0]], pivot k=0 with guess x0=1,y0=0. x1 = D[1][0] = 0, y1 = D[0][1] = 0, verified; output 'row 0' (or the equally valid 'col 0').
note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. Brute force over all row/column subsets for N<=3 agreed on existence and validity. Sample 3 output differs but is valid.

brief: Boxes hold a_i pieces; move pieces between neighbours, one per second. Make every box count divisible by some k > 1 at minimum time, or report -1 if the total is 1.
key_idea: For a prime p dividing S = sum a_i, each boundary between boxes must end with a multiple of p; the cost at boundary i is min(r, p-r) where r is the prefix sum mod p, and the answer is the minimum over primes p dividing S.
solution:
1. If S = 1, print -1.
2. Factor S by trial division up to sqrt(S) (S <= 1e12).
3. For each prime p: sum over i < n of min(pref_i mod p, p - pref_i mod p).
4. Output the minimum over primes.
complexity: O(n * w(S) + sqrt(S)) time, where w(S) is the number of distinct primes; O(1) extra space
dry_run: Sample 2: S=21, primes 3 and 7. For p=3 the prefixes 3,13,15,16 give residues 0,1,0,1, costs 0,1,0,1, total 2. p=7 is larger, so the answer is 2 (matches).
note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. All four samples match; the prime-boundary formula is the standard editorial one.

brief: Resources with goals a_i; producing one unit per turn; milestones (s,t,u) give a free unit of u when resource s reaches t. After each of q updates to the milestone set, print the minimum turns.
key_idea: Every milestone with t < a_s always fires, since count of s passes through t, so the free units are fixed; the turns needed equal the sum over resources of max(0, a_i - F_i), where F_i is the number of active milestones rewarding i.
solution:
1. Store milestones in a map keyed by (s,t); count F_u for active ones (t < a_s).
2. Keep total = sum max(0, a_i - F_i) and adjust it by the change in one term per update.
3. On each update, remove the old milestone at (s,t) if present, then insert the new one if u != 0.
4. Print total after each update.
complexity: O(q log q + n) time, O(n + q) space

note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. All five sample outputs match.

brief: Tree with n stations; m passenger records each give a path and the minimum beauty on it. Assign each edge a value in [1,1e6] satisfying all records, or print -1.
key_idea: Each edge's smallest allowed value is the maximum g over records covering it; using exactly these values is optimal, and then each record is satisfied iff its path minimum equals g.
solution:
1. Root the tree at 1 by BFS; store parent, parent edge and depth.
2. For each record, walk its path by climbing from the deeper endpoint; set L[e] = max(L[e], g).
3. For each record, check that the minimum of L on the path equals g; if not, print -1.
4. Otherwise print L (uncovered edges use 1).

note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. Samples 1-3 agree (sample 3 gives -1); validity of the output is checked by construction.

brief: Tanks with volumes a_i; repeatedly replace a contiguous segment by its average. Output the lexicographically smallest reachable sequence.
key_idea: Lexicographically smallest is achieved by a stack of blocks whose averages strictly increase; merge the new element into the top block while the top average is at least the new average.
solution:
1. Scan left to right, pushing (sum, count) for the current element.
2. While the stack top's average >= the current block's average, merge them (compare sum1*cnt2 >= sum2*cnt1 in integers).
3. Push the merged block.
4. Print each block's average once per element.
dry_run: Sample 1: 7,5,5,7. Push 7; 5 merges (7>=5) into avg 6; next 5 merges (6>=5) into 17/3; 7 does not merge. Output 5.666667 x3, 7.000000 (matches).
note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. Samples 1-3 match to 9 decimals.

brief: Connected graph with edge prices; Mike travels a->b->c, paying each traversal. Assign the prices to edges to minimise his cheapest trip cost.
key_idea: For a meeting vertex v, the trip is a->v, v->b (twice), v->c; cheapest prices go to the doubled segment, giving cost pref[dA+dB+dC] + pref[dB] over sorted prices.
solution:
1. BFS from a, b and c (unweighted distances).
2. Sort prices; prefix sums pref.
3. For each vertex v with dA+dB+dC <= m: candidate = pref[dA+dB+dC] + pref[dB].
4. Print the minimum candidate.
5. The dA+dB+dC <= m guard skips vertices whose three paths would need overlapping edges.
complexity: O(n + m + m log m) time per test, O(n + m) space
dry_run: Sample 1: star with centre 1; a=2,b=3,c=4; prices sorted 1,2,3. v=1: dA=dB=dC=1, cost = pref[3] + pref[1] = 6 + 1 = 7 (matches).
note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. Samples 1-2 match. The overlap guard is a heuristic; random brute force over price permutations on small graphs (150 cases) agreed. Treat as medium.

brief: Pillars with heights h_i; add a brick (A), remove a brick (R) or move a brick between pillars (M). Make all heights equal at minimum total cost.
key_idea: For a target height H, bricks to add Q and remove P are fixed; min(P,Q) moves at cost min(M, A+R) and the rest at A or R. The cost is piecewise linear in H, so only the h_i values and floor/ceil of the average need checking.
solution:
1. Sort heights; prefix sums.
2. For target H, Q = H*count(h<H) - sum(h<H), P = sum(h>H) - H*count(h>H).
3. cost(H) = min(P,Q)*min(M,A+R) + (P>Q ? (P-Q)*R : (Q-P)*A).
4. Evaluate cost at each h_i and at floor/ceil of sum/N; print the minimum.
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
dry_run: Sample 4 (N=5, A=1, R=2, M=4), H=5: heights 3 -> Q=2, 6 -> P=1. min(P,Q)*min(4,3)=3, plus (2-1)*A=1, total 4 (matches).
note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. All five samples match.

brief: Connected graph with n vertices and integer k. Output an independent set of size ceil(k/2) or a simple cycle of length at most k.
key_idea: The first k vertices visited by BFS from 1 induce a connected subgraph; if that subgraph is a tree, its larger bipartition class is independent; otherwise a non-tree edge closes a cycle of length at most k.
solution:
1. BFS from 1 and take the first k vertices as set S.
2. BFS inside S to get a tree with depths and parents.
3. If some edge inside S is not a tree edge, climb from its ends to their LCA to get the cycle.
4. Otherwise 2-colour by depth parity and output ceil(k/2) vertices of the larger class.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
dry_run: Sample 4 (n=5, k=5): BFS order 1..5 is a tree. Depth parity classes {1,4,5} and {2,3}. Output 1 4 5 (matches).
note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. Samples 1, 2, 4 match in form (any valid answer accepted); 150 random graphs checked by a validator.

brief: Two binary strings of equal length; one operation rotates a chosen subsequence clockwise. Give the minimum number of operations to turn s into t, or -1.
key_idea: Mismatch positions contribute +1 (s=1) or -1 (s=0) to a running balance; the answer is the maximum absolute prefix balance, and it is -1 if the counts of ones differ.
solution:
1. If the number of ones in s and t differ, print -1.
2. Scan positions; at each mismatch add +1 if s[i]=1 else -1.
3. Track the maximum of |balance|.
4. Print the maximum.

note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied verbatim. Brute-force BFS over rotations for n<=5 agreed on all random cases; all four samples match.

brief: Binary string with '?' characters; every pair 01 costs x and every pair 10 costs y. Replace each '?' with 0 or 1 to minimise the total.
key_idea: An optimal fill is a threshold: a prefix of the '?' positions takes one value and the rest take the other; sweep the flips and update the cost in O(1) from prefix counts.
solution:
1. Build prefix counts of fixed 0s, fixed 1s and '?'.
2. For each start value v (all '?' = v), compute the cost in O(n).
3. Flip the '?' positions one by one from left to right to the other value; the delta uses the zeros/ones before and after the position.
4. Track the minimum over all states.

brief: Ability deals a damage at time t and heals b at each of t+1..t+c, usable every d seconds. Find the largest starting health the enemy can be killed from, or -1 if unbounded.
key_idea: With casts at 0, d, 2d, ... the damage-minus-heal value after j casts is concave in j; if a > b*c the answer is unbounded, otherwise the optimum is at j = floor((a-1)/(b*d)).
solution:
1. If a > b*c, print -1 (each extra cast nets positive damage forever).
2. Otherwise let j = (a-1)/(b*d).
3. Answer = a*(j+1) - b*d*j*(j+1)/2.
4. Derivation: heal at time T is applied before damage at T (fixed by the samples).
note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied from the fetch. All seven samples match. The ordering (heal before damage at the same tick) is inferred from samples, since the fetched summary said otherwise.

brief: Array a of length n. Split into three non-empty consecutive parts with lengths x,y,z such that max of part 1, min of part 2 and max of part 3 are equal. Output any split or NO.
key_idea: Fix the left end l of the middle part; the common value must be the prefix max of a[1..l-1]; then the middle can extend right only while elements stay >= v, must include an occurrence of v, and the suffix max must equal v.
solution:
1. Prefix max pm and suffix max sm; RMQ over a.
2. For each l in 2..n-1 let v = pm[l-1].
3. R = last index before the first element < v after l; f = first occurrence of v at or after l; need f <= R.
4. Find smallest t in [f+1, R+1] with sm[t] <= v (binary search); if sm[t] == v, set r = t-1 and output (l-1, r-l+1, n-r).
5. Otherwise print NO.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n log n) space (sparse table)

note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied from the fetch. Brute force over all splits on random arrays (n<=8) agreed.

brief: Set of n distinct vectors over GF(2) with m coordinates, each with at most two ones. Output |T| mod 1e9+7 (T = all XOR sums) and the lexicographically smallest minimal generating subset.
key_idea: Treat coordinate 0 as ground: a vector with two coordinates is an edge, a single coordinate is an edge to ground; greedy DSU in index order gives the basis, so |T| = 2^rank.
solution:
1. DSU over nodes 0..m with node 0 as ground.
2. For each vector i in order: u, v (v = 0 if single coordinate); if find(u) != find(v), union and keep i.
3. rank r = number of kept vectors; |T| = 2^r mod p.
4. Print r and the kept indices (already sorted).
complexity: O((n + m) alpha) time, O(n + m) space

brief: x red and y blue candies; a gift set is a red + b blue or a blue + b red. Maximise the number of sets.
key_idea: With a >= b, k sets are feasible iff k*b <= min(x,y) and some integer count p of the first set type satisfies both colour limits; feasibility is monotone in k, so binary search on k.
solution:
1. Swap a and b so a >= b.
2. Binary search k in [0, (x+y)/(a+b)].
3. For k: need k*b <= min(x,y). If a == b, this is enough.
4. Else L = max(0, k - (y-k*b)/(a-b)), R = min(k, (x-k*b)/(a-b)); feasible iff L <= R.
5. Print the largest feasible k.
dry_run: Sample 1 (x=10,y=12,a=5,b=2): k=3 gives L=1, R=1 (feasible); k=4 gives L=3 > R=0. Answer 3 (matches).
note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied from the fetch. All nine samples match. Brute force over the two set-type counts on random small inputs agreed.

brief: Tree game: a token moves to an unvisited neighbour u of v when u XOR v <= min(u,v). Relabel the nodes so that every starting node wins for the first player, and print that permutation.
key_idea: Give every node a label so that adjacent labels have different highest set bits; then u XOR v > min(u,v) on every edge, nobody can move, and every start wins.
solution:
1. 2-colour the tree by BFS from node 1; c0 = size of colour 0.
2. Groups G_k = [2^k, 2^(k+1)-1] capped at n; they partition 1..n.
3. Subset-DP over group sizes to find groups whose total size is exactly c0.
4. Colour-0 nodes take labels from the chosen groups, colour-1 nodes take the rest.
5. Print labels; any valid permutation is accepted.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n log n) space per test

brief: Participants have weights a_i in [1,n]. Choose x<y to split into light (<x), middle ([x,y)) and heavy (>=y); each group count must be a non-zero power of two. Minimise the number of invitations.
key_idea: Cost is the sum of P(c) - c over groups, with P(c) the smallest power of two >= max(c,1); for each light cut and heavy power bucket, the smallest feasible middle cut is optimal.
solution:
1. Sort weights; valid cut positions are where the value changes (plus 0 and n).
2. For each valid light cut p and each k in 0..18, take the smallest valid middle cut q >= max(p, n-2^k) (q > p unless the gap allows an empty middle).
3. Candidate = P(p) + P(q-p) + P(n-q) - n.
4. Print the minimum over candidates.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

note: Fetched statement is a paraphrase; samples copied from the fetch. All four samples match. The empty-middle case is covered by the gap condition; random brute force over all integer (x,y) agreed.

brief: Array of n non-negative integers, at most k changes. Cost = DIFF - MEX; output the minimum cost after at most k changes.
key_idea: For a target MEX m, the cost equals the number of distinct values > m that survive; the changes must cover all copies of m and fill the missing values below m, and the rest of the budget removes the rarest big values, found with a BIT over counts.
solution:
1. Count values <= n; keep larger values in a BIT indexed by their count.
2. For m = 0..n: remove value m from the BIT (big = values > m).
3. Feasible if cnt[m] <= k and miss(m) <= k, where miss(m) = m - distinct values in [0,m).
4. budget = k - cnt[m]; take the rarest big values whose total count fits the budget (BIT descent).
5. Cost = (#big distinct) - (#removed); answer = min over m.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
